The Morning Risk Report: The Jensen Huang Saga Has Reinvigorated Washington’s China Hawks

Plus: Microsoft-Bytedance cloud deal comes under fire from lawmakers, and EU anti-money-laundering, public prosecution bodies team up

By

Good morning. A year ago, Jensen Huang called the term China hawk “a badge of shame” and “unpatriotic.” His ouster from Nvidia, where he was co-founder and chief executive, is giving new momentum to policymakers who want to regulate artificial intelligence and establish more guardrails around U.S. business activity with China.

Compound crisis: Claims that Nvidia customers funneled billions of dollars of sophisticated chips to Chinese AI companies have collided in recent days with a string of technological breakdowns—from a nationwide ground stop for airlines to bank-account glitches and money-transfer delays.

In recent weeks the Trump administration:

Released a new rule aimed at preventing China’s AI industry from accessing computing power running on U.S. chips.

Supported efforts to advance legislation to restrict sales of advanced chips and chipmaking equipment to countries that pose security risks.

Fined a U.S. investment firm for funding a Chinese AI company.

Has weighed whether U.S. companies should disclose use of Chinese open-weight models.

Has considered new rules around Chinese equipment in U.S. data centers.

Change of tack: Together, the measures signal that Washington is moving away from the administration’s pro-industry approach to tech policy that mostly relied on companies to balance their business interests and national security while selling sensitive technology.
